To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

tumor oxygenation can be explained by growth and compression of blood vessels, that the latter can cause resistance to chemotherapy and that this is in agreement with recent clinical data on breast cancer.

the reported higher average hemoglobulin concentration of tumors is due to tumor vessel dilatation and the reported lower average oxygen hemoglobin concentration of some tumors is due to intra-tumoral vessel compression.

tumor hemoglobin concentrations are elevated because of tumor vessel dilatation, whereas tumor blood oxygenation is below normal because of compression of tumor vessels by intra-tumorous solid stress.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a computational model for tumor vascularization, blood flow and oxygen transport, which is applied to clinical data of hemoglobin concentrations in breast cancer patients.
the question whether the spatially resolved oxygenation of tumors and host tissue can be predicted based on the tumor vascular architecture and tumor growth.
the development of a computational model for oxygen transport in tumors and host tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the reported data on hemoglobin and oxy- to total concentration are consistent with a model of tumor vascularization by cooption, angiogenetic growth, and regression, which includes compression of blood vessels during tumor growth.

the reported data on hemoglobin concentrations of breast tumors can only be explained by assuming a heterogeneous tumor vascularization and a heterogeneous distribution of tumor compartments with varying capillary densities.
tumors with oxyhemoglobin concentration below normal should be considered for chemotherapy whereas tumors with oxyhemogolbin concentration above normal may be considered for radio- or immunotherapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

our modeling results suggest a strong correlation of tumor blood flow with the ability of the tumor to respond to chemotherapy and that the tumor blood flow can be estimated from measurements of oxy- and total tumor hemoglobin concentration.
tumor oxygenation is a complex phenomenon, depending on tumor and associated normal tissue vascular geometry, blood flow, hematological properties, and tumor metabolism.
the model can qualitatively explain the reported optical mammography data and suggests that the observed tumor oxy-to total hemoglobulin concentrations can be related to tumor vessel geometry.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatially heterogeneous oxygenation of tumors is not only a result of the tumor vasculatures geometry but also of the tumor vasculo-architecture and its dynamics.
the oxygenation of breast cancer tumors cannot be predicted based on the oxygenation of the surrounding host tissue.
a simple computational model can explain the reported data of optical mammographic measurements of hemoglobin concentrations and blood oxygenation in human breast tumors.
